figures.finding: In France in 2024, the CNC approved (agréé) 309 feature films: 244 fiction, 52 documentaries and 13 animation; 231 of them were French-initiative (FIF).
figures.applies: France, films approved for production by the CNC, 2019-2024; the CNC's approval genres are only fiction, documentary and animation.
figures.use: A French-initiative production's form (fiction, documentary, animation) is drawn against these approval counts, so a documentary or animated feature is the rarer, harder-to-place project in France.

figures.finding: In French cinemas in 2024, comedies took 22.3% of admissions to first-run films from 13.0% of releases, animation 19.4% from 8.1%, adventure 18.5% from 5.9%, and documentaries 1.7% from 18.4%; drama was 29.8% of releases.

value.unit: share of admissions to first-run films vs share of releases

figures.applies: France, first-run features only (82% to 94% of admissions by year); 2024 data provisional.
figures.use: A film's French box office draws on its genre's admissions per release (share of admissions over share of releases): comedy, animation and adventure earn above their weight, documentary far below.

figures.use: A film's UK box office draws on its genre's share of gross per release here; the BFI's genre list (18 genres) maps to the game's genres by name.

figures.finding: Of the writers, directors and top-billed stars of the 2,600 top-grossing US/Canada films of 2000-2025, roughly a quarter had family already in film or TV before they joined: stars 28%, directors 26%, writers 18%.

value.unit: share with a parent or close blood relative in film/TV before entry

figures.applies: Top ~100 US/Canada grossing films per year, 2000-2025; shares of people whose family background could be established.
figures.use: The share of lives born to a family in the business is drawn by role from these figures (an actor's family more often than a writer's), so the family trade is a weighted draw, not an even one.

sources.said: Of the people I studied, roughly a quarter had a family member already in the film or TV industry before they joined. Top-billed actors lead on 28%. Directors are close behind on 26%. Writers come out lower, on 18%
30% of top films have no nepo baby anywhere in their core team. 36% carry exactly one, 23% carry two, and 11% have three or more.

figures.finding: Of 4,403 actors under 35 in US films of 2000-2025 whose family status could be confirmed, 28% (1,242) had at least one parent who worked in entertainment; of those, 60% had a parent in acting, 16% directing, 14% music, 9% producing, and 41% had two industry parents.

value.by_year: about 6-8% of young casts in the 2000s and 2010s, 16.6% by 2024 (as the report states)

figures.applies: Actors under 35 at release in US films 2000-2025 meeting a visibility criterion; a data company's own sample, which says it does not represent all working actors.
figures.use: Which trade an actor's industry parent had (acting most often) is drawn from these shares; a cross-check on Follows's 28% for stars.

sources.said: From 2000 to 2025, nepo babies made up 28% of confirmed young actors in U.S. movies, while 72% were non-nepo stars.
Directing was the second most common connection at 16%, followed by the music sector at 14% and producing at 9%.
Most nepo stars came from one-industry-parent households: 59% had one parent in entertainment, while 41% had two parents in the entertainment industry.
The confirmed-status sample included 4,403 actors under age 35, of whom 1,242 were confirmed nepo actors.

figures.finding: Gorji, Carney and Prakash (2020) find, on IMDb data for Hollywood show-business families, strong support that third-party network sponsorship benefits relatives' careers, more so for women, alongside the continuing importance of direct family preferment.

value.effect: sponsorship by family associates significantly benefits relatives' career performance; accentuated for women; direct preferment also matters

figures.applies: Hollywood movie industry, show-business family relatives (abstract only; the full text is paywalled).
figures.use: A family in the business works through the people the family knows (a contact who sponsors the player), which is how the game's contacts engine should carry it.

sources.said: We find strong support for our sponsorship hypotheses, but we also note the continuing importance of direct forms of family preferment in an industry characterized by single project organizations and boundaryless careers.

figures.finding: In UK film, TV, video, radio and photography, 12.4% of workers had working-class parents (NS-SEC 6-8) against 35% of the whole workforce, and 25.8% had parents in higher managerial and professional jobs (NS-SEC 1) against 13.7%; music, performing and visual art: 18.2% and 28.9%.

value.unit: share of workers by parents' NS-SEC

figures.applies: UK, Labour Force Survey (Oakley, Laurison, O'Brien and Friedman 2017), as tabled in Panic! 2018.
figures.use: The family's trade sets its class by NS-SEC, and a working-class family is about a third as common among the game's screen workers as in the population, which the background draw should reflect.

figures.finding: At the BFI Film Fund (2017-2022), applicants from middle-class backgrounds were more successful at the Development stage: 43% of middle-class writers succeeded against 25% of working-class writers, and producers 44% against 21%; only 4% of Development awards went to working-class producers.

value.applicants_managerial_professional_share: two thirds, against 37% of the workforce

figures.applies: UK, applicants to the BFI Film Fund (NETWORK, Development, Production strands), 2017-2022, class by parental occupation.
figures.use: Where the game models a UK public fund's decision, the applicant's class of origin moves the success rate by these published rates (the paper reports them; it does not claim class causes them).

sources.said: As seen in Table 4, for instance, 43% of middle class writers who apply for Development funds are successful, compared to 25% of working class writers.
Development Producer 44 40 21 Director 42 29 31 Writer 43 37 25
In total, only 4% of awards to the Development fund go to producers from working class backgrounds.
Overall, two thirds of applicants are from managerial/professional backgrounds, as compared with 37% of the total workforce from this background in 2022.

sources.title: Stephen Follows, What percentage of Hollywood film professionals are nepo babies?, 10 Aug 2026
sources.basis: Stephen Follows's own dataset: biographies of 6,921 writers, directors and top-3 billed actors of the ~100 top-grossing US/Canada releases of each year 2000-2025 (2,600 films); family = parent or close blood relative in film/TV before the person's entry; background established for 87% of directors, 76% of stars, 37% of writers
sources.said: Of the people I studied, roughly a quarter had a family member already in the film or TV industry before they joined. Top-billed actors lead on 28%. Directors are close behind on 26%. Writers come out lower, on 18% … 30% of top films have no nepo baby anywhere in their core team. 36% carry exactly one, 23% carry two, and 11% have three or more. … Connected directors get their first film made younger (a median age of 33 against 35), and those who eventually reached the top 100 climbed faster (a median of 8 years from first feature against 10). Most of all, they get more chances. 72% went on to a second feature against 66% of everyone else, and their median career is three features against two. … Films directed by industry-family directors have a median adjusted domestic gross of $84m, compared with $87m for films directed by everyone else.
